Estate liquidity: a positive eventual balance can still hide an immediate cash gap

Four graphics reconcile accessible cash, later asset-sale receipts, immediate obligations and dated payments without confusing a cash forecast with an estate distribution.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 4 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Explore an estate cash-timing ledger

Interactive planning lab

Maximum additional cash needed$67,000
Total entered obligations over 24 months$116,000
Ending cash position after 24 months$159,000

Hypothetical estate-only cash ledger over 24 months. Starting cash is assumed legally accessible; immediate obligations settle at time zero. The selected asset-sale receipt arrives at the start of its month, with recurring costs and the separate tax/debt payment at month-end. Sale cash is net of sale costs and secured loans but before the separate tax/debt payment entered here. No estate distribution, other asset valuation, interest, borrowing cost, tax assessment, probate calculation or claim priority is determined. Dates and amounts are placeholders, not legal deadlines or processing-time estimates. A positive cash position does not authorize distribution.

The central idea

List amounts and access dates separately. Assets expected to become cash later may leave immediate costs unfunded, even when the ledger ends with a positive balance.

01

Distinguish an asset from money available to pay an invoice

An estate can have valuable property while lacking cash for a bill due now. Access, sale timing, secured debt and administrative requirements affect when an amount becomes usable. British Columbia’s estate guide describes duties including listing assets and debts, paying valid obligations, filing returns and preparing accounts. Its guidance is specific to B.C.; other jurisdictions have their own requirements.

This illustration tracks estate cash only. Starting cash is assumed accessible to the authorized representative, and a later asset sale supplies a separate receipt. No personal money from an executor or beneficiary is automatically included.

The sale input means cash after selling costs and secured loans, before the separate tax and debt payment entered in the controls. It is not the gross property value. Entering a liability in both the net-sale figure and the separate payment would count the same obligation twice.

02

Put immediate and recurring obligations on a calendar

The example starts with CAD 25,000 of accessible cash and CAD 20,000 of immediate obligations, leaving CAD 5,000 at time zero. It then pays CAD 1,500 of carrying and administration costs each month for twenty-four months.

A separate CAD 60,000 payment is scheduled at the end of month six. This input is a placeholder for a separately estimated tax or debt obligation. The model does not calculate an actual liability, determine claim priority or assign a statutory deadline.

The later net sale receipt is CAD 250,000 in month nine. Under the model’s explicit convention, receipts arrive at the beginning of their selected month and bills settle at month-end. Actual settlement dates within a month can matter, so a monthly ledger should not replace a dated payment list when the margin is tight.

03

Read the deepest shortage as well as the endpoint

The selected cash path falls below zero before the sale. At the end of month six, after the separate payment, the position is negative CAD 64,000. Continuing carrying costs take it to negative CAD 67,000 after month eight, just before the modeled month-nine receipt.

The maximum-additional-cash metric is therefore CAD 67,000. It is the amount which, if available at the start without interest or repayment, would keep this selected ledger from falling below zero. The tool does not establish that borrowing, an advance or any other funding source is available.

The comparison curve moves the same receipt up to three months earlier while keeping every amount unchanged. A different receipt date can reduce the peak funding need even though the final balance remains identical. The curves connect month-end observations; they do not show every intra-month movement.

04

Reconcile the totals without calling the remainder distributable

The totals waterfall adds CAD 25,000 of starting cash and CAD 250,000 of later proceeds, then subtracts CAD 20,000 of immediate obligations, CAD 36,000 of recurring costs and the separate CAD 60,000 payment. It ends at CAD 159,000.

That positive endpoint coexists with the earlier CAD 67,000 funding gap. Neither figure measures the full estate’s legal solvency or the amount beneficiaries may receive. Assets and obligations outside this ledger, later assessments, unresolved claims and professional costs could change the result.

The CRA’s clearance-certificate guidance explains the representative’s tax exposure when assets are distributed without clearance and tax remains owing. A positive cash forecast does not replace clearance, legal advice or the other requirements applicable to a distribution.

05

Stress the dates and document the assumptions

The matrix changes the sale-receipt month and the separate payment month. Each cell finds the deepest cash shortage over the full twenty-four-month ledger after counting starting cash. Immediate obligations and monthly costs remain fixed. Same-month receipts precede bills by convention.

Use the grid to identify a dependency that needs verification: a planned receipt may need confirmed authority, a completed sale and accessible settlement funds. The selected dates are neither predicted processing times nor permission to postpone an obligation.

The ledger includes no interest on borrowing and no investment return on temporary cash. It assumes the monthly costs continue for the whole horizon and includes no beneficiary distribution. A practical review replaces placeholders with supported amounts and dates, records what remains uncertain, and checks who has authority to act before treating an apparent funding solution as available.
